readerTitle: Why collecting all the data first can leave you with no answer
caseNote: 가상 사례 (가정 청소 업체, 대형 소매업체 고객지원팀) · 의사의 감별 진단과 컨설팅의 가설 주도 문제 해결은 일반적 관행으로만 언급
insight: 데이터를 모으기 전에 '가장 그럴듯한 답'을 먼저 적으면, 무엇을 볼지와 무엇을 무시해도 되는지가 정해진다.
misconception: 선입견 없이 데이터를 전부 모아 보면 답이 저절로 드러난다. 추측부터 하는 것은 비과학적이다.

sources.text: Rasiel, E. (1999). The McKinsey Way. McGraw-Hill. (초기 가설로 문제 해결을 시작하는 방식)
의학의 감별 진단(differential diagnosis): 가능한 원인 목록을 세우고 검사로 좁혀 가는 표준 임상 관행
청소 업체와 고객지원팀 사례 및 모든 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 청소 업체 사례(예약 15% 감소, 3주, 40개 열 스프레드시트)와 고객지원팀 사례(처리 시간 30% 증가, 티켓 12,000건)는 모두 설명용 가상 수치입니다.
6번 카드의 의사 비유는 감별 진단의 일반적 설명입니다. 특정 연구 수치는 인용하지 않았습니다. 의학 감수자에게 표현이 과장되지 않았는지 확인받으세요.
컨설팅 회사들이 가설 주도 접근을 가르친다는 서술은 Rasiel(1999) 등에 근거한 일반적 서술입니다. 특정 회사의 내부 교육 내용으로 단정하지 않도록 카드에서 회사명을 쓰지 않았습니다.

cards.title: Three weeks of data. No answer.
body: Maria runs a home cleaning company. Bookings fell 15% in two months, so she did the careful thing: she pulled every number she had.
Three weeks later she had a spreadsheet with 40 columns and still no idea what was wrong. The problem wasn't too little data. It was starting without a guess.

image.label: Owner buried in a huge spreadsheet
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 작은 사무실 책상에 앉은 청소 업체 사장이 바닥까지 늘어진 거대한 스프레드시트 출력물에 파묻혀 있음. 책상 옆에 청소 도구 바구니. 실제 브랜드 로고 없음.

cards.title: Bookings are down 15%. Where do you start?
body: You run a cleaning company with 12 cleaners and about 300 regular customers. Bookings have dropped for two months. You have a few days to spare on this.
What do you do first?

options.text: Pull every report and survey all customers, then look for patterns
options.feedback: Thorough, but slow. Without knowing what you're looking for, most of that data won't point anywhere.

options.text: Write down your best guess at the cause, then find the quickest check that could prove it wrong
options.feedback: You may guess wrong, but you'll know within days. Each check either answers the question or rules out a cause.

options.text: Cut prices 10% now, since price is the usual reason
options.feedback: Fast action, but it's a guess you never tested. If price isn't the cause, you lose margin and bookings stay down.

cards.title: One guess did what 40 columns couldn't.
body: A friend asked Maria a simple question: what changed two months ago? She had reshuffled cleaner schedules to cut travel time.

That gave her a guess: *customers who lost their regular cleaner stopped booking.* She checked it in one afternoon, comparing rebooking rates for customers who kept their cleaner with those who didn't.
The gap was large. The answer had been in her data all along. She just hadn't known which two columns to compare.

image.label: Two groups of customers compared side by side
image.brief: 간단한 인포그래픽. 왼쪽은 'Kept their cleaner' 그룹(집 아이콘 대부분 초록 체크), 오른쪽은 'Got a new cleaner' 그룹(집 아이콘 다수가 회색으로 빠짐). 숫자는 넣지 않음.

cards.title: Start with a hypothesis
body: A **hypothesis** is your best guess at the answer, stated clearly enough that evidence could prove it wrong. You write it down *before* you collect data.
It isn't a conclusion. It's a tool for deciding what to look at. Facts are endless. A guess tells you which few matter, and which you can ignore for now.
Maria's data didn't change. Her question did.

cards.title: Guess, then try to break it.
body: A hypothesis is useful only if you test it quickly. The loop is short:
list: **State it:** "Bookings fell because customers lost their regular cleaner."
**If true, you'd see:** those customers rebook far less often
**If false, you'd see:** no difference between the groups
**Run the cheapest check** that tells the two apart
**Keep, revise or drop it,** then guess again
cards.callout: A wrong guess dropped in a day is progress, not failure.
cards.softwareNote: If sign-ups fall, guess first: "the new pricing page confuses people." Then compare conversion before and after the change, instead of building a dashboard of every metric.

cards.title: Good diagnosticians guess early.
body: A doctor seeing a patient with chest pain doesn't order every test in the hospital. She lists the likely causes, then orders the tests that can tell them apart. Doctors call this a differential diagnosis.
Many consulting teams work the same way, writing a first answer on day one and spending the project trying to prove or disprove it.
Collecting everything feels open-minded. In practice, it often means drowning before you know what you're looking for.

cards.title: A guess can harden into a belief.
body: Once you've written a hypothesis, you'll want it to be right. That's how people end up noticing only the evidence that agrees.
Two habits help. Write down two or three competing guesses, not one. And decide in advance what result would make you drop yours.
If you know almost nothing about an area, spend a short time exploring first. A hypothesis needs some grounding to be a good guess.

cards.title: Now you lead a support team.
body: You manage customer support inside a large retailer. Average time to resolve a ticket rose 30% this quarter. Your director wants an explanation by Friday.
Last quarter the company changed its returns policy and you hired four new agents. What's your plan?

options.text: Audit all 12,000 tickets from this quarter across every field
options.feedback: You might find the cause, but probably not by Friday. Without a guess, you won't know which fields to compare.

options.text: Guess it's the returns policy, and also test new agents. Compare resolve times by ticket type and agent tenure
options.feedback: Two competing guesses, each with a quick check. You'll likely have an answer in a day, and you'll know which one is wrong.

options.text: Tell the director it's the new hires and book extra training
options.feedback: Confident and quick, but untested. If returns tickets are the real cause, training won't help and you've blamed your new team.

cards.title: Guess first. Then try to prove yourself wrong.
body: A clear best guess turns a pile of data into a few useful checks.
**Try it today:** pick one problem you're stuck on. Write one sentence that starts "I think the cause is…" and one check that would prove it wrong.
